interviewQuestions.question: You're told a cache's miss rate is too high. How do you figure out whether it's a compulsory, capacity, or conflict problem, and what would you do about each?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd diagnose by varying the one parameter each category is sensitive to and watching how the miss rate responds, rather than guessing from the number alone. Compulsory misses happen on the very first touch of a block regardless of cache size or associativity — they're unavoidable structurally, so the only lever is hiding their latency with prefetching, not shrinking their count. Capacity misses persist even at full associativity, because the working set genuinely doesn't fit; the test is simulating (or measuring via a cache size sweep) the same access pattern at higher associativity but fixed capacity — if the miss rate barely moves, it's capacity, and the fix is either a bigger cache or restructuring the algorithm to shrink the working set (loop tiling, streaming instead of materializing). Conflict misses *do* disappear as associativity increases at fixed capacity, because they're caused by too many active blocks mapping to the same set — the fix there is more ways per set, or in software, padding/restructuring data layout to break an unlucky stride that collides in the index bits.

Concretely, I'd run the same trace at 1-way, 4-way, and fully-associative with capacity held constant. A miss rate that barely changes across all three is dominated by capacity or compulsory; one that drops sharply with associativity is conflict-dominated. Separating compulsory from capacity is harder from measurement alone — compulsory misses scale with the number of distinct blocks touched (roughly working-set size / block size for a cold start), so comparing a cold-cache run to a warm one isolates it.

**Testing:** a concrete, testable diagnostic method — varying associativity and comparing cold vs warm — not just recitation of three definitions.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Diagnosing miss rate

interviewQuestions.question: What's the fourth C, and why did the original three-Cs model need it?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The original three Cs — compulsory, capacity, conflict — implicitly assumed a single core with no outside interference: every miss was caused by *this* program's own access pattern against a private cache. Multicore systems with shared caches (a shared L3, or coherence traffic between private caches) broke that assumption, so the model added **coherence misses**: misses caused by another core invalidating a line you were using, not by anything your own access pattern did.

A coherence miss looks identical to a conflict or capacity miss from inside a single thread's counters — the line just isn't there anymore — but the cause and the fix are completely different. A capacity miss is fixed by making your own working set smaller or the cache bigger; a coherence miss is fixed by reducing cross-core interference on the same lines — eliminating false sharing, reducing how often multiple cores touch the same data, or restructuring a data structure so writers and readers on different cores don't collide on one line.

The practical consequence: profiling a multicore workload with only the classic three Cs in mind can send you chasing capacity or conflict fixes (bigger cache, better associativity) for a problem that's actually about which *other* core is touching your lines — those fixes won't move the needle, while eliminating false sharing or reducing shared-line contention will.

**Testing:** whether you know the three-Cs model predates multicore coherence and can name the failure mode it misses.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: The 4th C: coherence misses

interviewQuestions.question: Two functions have identical working-set sizes but very different conflict-miss rates. What in the code would cause that?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Conflict misses come from too many simultaneously-live blocks mapping into the *same set*, which is a function of address bits, not raw working-set size — so two data structures of identical total size can collide very differently depending on their stride relative to the cache's set count.

The classic trigger is a power-of-two stride that aligns badly with a power-of-two number of sets. Walking a matrix column-major with a row length that's a multiple of the cache's number of sets (a common case when dimensions are powers of two, e.g. a 1024x1024 float matrix on a cache with 1024 sets) makes every element in a column map to the *same* set — the working set is small, but that one set thrashes constantly while every other set sits idle. A second function touching the same total bytes but with a stride that isn't a multiple of the set count spreads accesses evenly across sets and sees almost no conflict misses despite an identical footprint.

The fix that shows up repeatedly in real code is padding: adding a small offset to a matrix's row stride (allocating `width + 1` columns instead of exactly a power of two) breaks the alignment and spreads the accesses back across sets, often cutting miss rate dramatically without changing the algorithm at all. Higher associativity also masks it, since more ways per set means more colliding blocks can coexist before eviction — which is exactly the associativity-sweep test for distinguishing conflict from capacity misses.

**Testing:** whether you can connect a concrete stride/alignment pattern to conflict misses, not just define the category abstractly.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Same footprint, different conflicts
